newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bougainville peace talks begin in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Bougainville peace talks begin in NZ.

text.p: Warring groups from Papua New Guinea's Bougainville island began formal talks in New Zealand on Monday in the hope of finding a solution to nine years of secessionist violence.

About 50 representatives of rival Bougainvillean factions came to Burnham Military Camp, near the South Island city of Christchurch, on Saturday for the peace talks, which are expected to last for at least a week.
Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon said the New Zealand government deliberately brought members of both groups together two days before formal discussions were due to begin.

"We intentionally wanted to bring them in and give them a chance to settle down with each other a little bit because in many cases there has been a bit of anger between them and, secondly, many of them haven't seen each other for a long time," McKinnon told Radio New Zealand.

"They're very much on their own. We are not part of the talks. We're not setting any agenda for them. We just really want them to get together and hopefully develop some empathy between the two major groups there and see where they are at the end of the week."
A Foreign Affairs official told Reuters the government was still working to get another 14 delegates to the meeting.

About eight were representatives of the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) and its political wing, the Bougainville Interim Government (BIG), and the remainder were Papua New Guinea politicians from Bougainville, the official said.
Some of the BRA delegates were prevented from leaving Bougainville last week when the helicopter sent to pick them up was fired upon, apparently by their own side.

The BRA and BIG have been battling for independence from Papua New Guinea for nearly a decade and are pitted against the pro-Papua New Guinea Bougainville Transitional Government (BTG), also at the talks.
Thousands have died in the bloody conflict since landowners revolted in 1989 over environmental damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine and the royalties received from it.
The mine is owned by a unit of Anglo-Australian giant Rio Tinto Plc/Ltd.

Joseph Kabui, head of the Bougainville rebel delegation, and BTG Premier Gerard Sinato said there was a groundswell of feeling among their people to end the fighting and they were confident of making a breakthrough.
"We do not expect a quick answer to the Bougainville crisis, which has divided our people and brought us suffering, sorrow and death," Sinato said.
"But we hope to strengthen our path to peace in our deliberations. We are in New Zealand to continue our search for lasting peace on Bougainville."
